entities.name: Julianus ben Sabar
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Julianus ben Sabar, a charismatic leader of the Samaritans, ignited a significant, albeit ultimately doomed, revolt against the Byzantine Empire in the early 6th century CE. Widely regarded by his followers as the Taheb – a messianic figure prophesied to restore Samaritan independence and purity – Julianus mobilized his community in 529 CE, challenging the escalating religious persecution and political marginalization imposed by Emperor Justinian I. His rebellion, centered in the heartland of Samaria, represented a desperate stand for cultural and religious autonomy in a period of intense imperial consolidation and Christianization, briefly threatening Byzantine control over parts of Palestine Prima.

The revolt, which erupted in the spring of 529 CE, saw Julianus ben Sabar's forces, composed largely of Samaritans and supported by some Jewish and Arab groups, seize control of Neapolis (modern Nablus), the spiritual center of Samaritanism. They massacred Christian residents, destroyed churches, and established a short-lived independent rule. Julianus was even crowned king, minting his own coinage, a profound symbolic act of defiance against imperial authority. The uprising quickly spread across Samaria, prompting a swift and brutal response from Justinian I. Byzantine general Theodoras, aided by Ghassanid Arab auxiliaries under King Harith ibn Jabalah, crushed the rebellion by 531 CE, capturing Julianus and executing him, reportedly after dismembering his body.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Julianus ben Sabar's revolt, though brief, triggered a demographic catastrophe for the Samaritan community, leading to their permanent decline as a major religious and political force in the Levant. It also solidified Justinian I's policy of religious uniformity, directly resulting in the oppressive Novel 109.
